First, we define the function.

```python
from typing import Dict, Optional
from urllib.parse import urljoin

import html2text
import httpx
from autogen_core.code_executor import ImportFromModule
from autogen_core.tools import FunctionTool
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup


async def fetch_webpage(
    url: str, include_images: bool = True, max_length: Optional[int] = None, headers: Optional[Dict[str, str]] = None
) -> str:
    """Fetch a webpage and convert it to markdown format.

    Args:
        url: The URL of the webpage to fetch
        include_images: Whether to include image references in the markdown
        max_length: Maximum length of the output markdown (if None, no limit)
        headers: Optional HTTP headers for the request

    Returns:
        str: Markdown version of the webpage content

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the URL is invalid or the page can't be fetched
    """
    # Use default headers if none provided
    if headers is None:
        headers = {"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36"}

    try:
        # Fetch the webpage
        async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
            response = await client.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=10)
            response.raise_for_status()

            # Parse HTML
            soup = BeautifulSoup(response.text, "html.parser")
.....

```

Then we create a FunctionTool from that and pass in the right parameters

```python

# Create the webpage fetching tool
fetch_webpage_tool = FunctionTool(
    func=fetch_webpage,
    description="Fetch a webpage and convert it to markdown format, with options for including images and limiting length",
    global_imports=[
        "os",
        "html2text",
        ImportFromModule("typing", ("Optional", "Dict")),
        "httpx",
        ImportFromModule("bs4", ("BeautifulSoup",)),
        ImportFromModule("html2text", ("HTML2Text",)),
        ImportFromModule("urllib.parse", ("urljoin",)),
    ],
)
```

This way, all the logic for dumping the tool is in the FunctionTool and should be dumped correctly.

body:
Hi, I managed to get a solution for my issue by overriding AssistantAgent with a new parameter that tells the Assistant to add a Terminate sequence when returning a TextMessage. The point is that models return TextMessage and not Handoffs mainly when the task is complete and there is a final answer for the user. 

Thus, I don't rely on the model to incorporate the Terminate sequence through prompting. And still when the task is not complete the Agent can Handoff to other Agents, including a UserProxy that involves human in the loop. The behaviour has been pretty consistent since this.

Still it is possible that Agents expected to always Handoff, try to deliver a final message.To avoid that the best solution that came to my mind was to be able to force tools usage in the model (as Handoffs are tools in the end). This should also allow a better experience for other use cases regarding tools.

And finally, using the Core API to design our own pattern would definitely work for the first point, with total control about the Handoffs. Only that it would take more time and complexity on the development.

> Hi! This exact feature is in PR right now, see here: [#5134](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/5134)

Hi @jackgerrits! thanks for having a read into the issue. Unfortunately, that PR isn't for the same scenario we are working on. Currently, we are trying to build a multiagent solution that targets a "production ready" environment. Based on different reads, SK is targeting a stable production ready framework. While AG, is up to date with latest research on the multi agent arena. 
We also understand that SK is bringing into their platform mature patterns from the AG framework. So, in our case, we are trying to be as close as possible to SK and take bring the orchestration that AG Standalone Runtime offers.

Now regarding the the difference between SK Agent and SK Kernel Service, from the doco:
#### Agent
- **Definition**: An agent in the Semantic Kernel framework is an entity that can participate in one or more conversations. It includes attributes like name, description, and instructions.
- **Functionality**: Agents define their communication protocols through an `AgentChannel` and can format instructions for the kernel. They can merge arguments and create communication channels.
- **Example**: `Agent` class in Python [source](https://github.com/microsoft/semantic-kernel/blob/main/python/semantic_kernel/agents/agent.py).
#### Kernel Service
- **Definition**: Kernel services extend the functionality of the Kernel by adding services related entities, including AI services.
- **Functionality**: Kernel services can select AI services, add, remove, and get services by ID or type. They manage services like `TextCompletionClientBase` and `ChatCompletionClientBase`.
- **Example**: `KernelServicesExtension` in Python [source](https://github.com/microsoft/semantic-kernel/blob/main/python/semantic_kernel/services/kernel_services_extension.py).

In summary, agents are responsible for handling interactions and communication protocols, while kernel services manage the underlying AI services and functionality within the Semantic Kernel framework.

So far from our research pointed out the PR from @lspinheiro and the existing adapter [SKChatCompletionAdapter ](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/python/packages/autogen-ext/src/autogen_ext/models/semantic_kernel/_sk_chat_completion_adapter.py#L32)

Hope it provides more clarity.

Thanks!

body:
@philippHorn the reason for not including the tools in the reflection step is because we want to force a text response. 

You can set `reflect_on_tool_use=False` to disable the second inference and repeatedly call the agent without a task or message to get agent to repeatedly execute tools. 

For model provider compatibility issue, is this only related to Open Router? Because if you use Gemini directly from `OpenAIChatCompletionClient` it works fine. 

A more complete fix would be to add `tool_choice` parameter in the `extra_create_args` in the reflection inference call, and set `tool_choice=None`. However, the syntax is only for OpenAI and not translated to other providers. https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat/create#chat-create-tool_choice. We will need to add a new `tool_choice` parameter to `ChatCompletionClient` base class for this to work.

body:
@surendransuri ,

## Use Streams and not Http Trigger

From the code I see above, it seems you are trying to stream output over a http connection in an Azure function. HTTP is stateless and not suitable for streaming. 

Now I found this documentation on supporting[ http streams](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/azurecompute/azure-functions-support-for-http-streams-in-python-is-now-in-preview/4146697) in azure python. Please read it . 

It seems that your code should look like this 

```python
import azure.functions as func
from azurefunctions.extensions.http.fastapi import Request, StreamingResponse

app = func.FunctionApp(http_auth_level=func.AuthLevel.ANONYMOUS)

async def stream_messages(result_stream):
    """Convert agent messages to SSE format"""
    async for msg in result_stream:
        if isinstance(msg, TaskResult):
            continue
        # Format the message as SSE data
        yield f"data: {msg.model_dump()}\n\n"

@app.route(route="chat", methods=[func.HttpMethod.POST])
async def chat_stream(req: Request) -> StreamingResponse:
    """Endpoint to stream chat responses"""
    task = req.query_params.get('task') or (await req.json()).get('task')
    
    agent_team = await get_selector_group_chat_team()
    result_stream = agent_team.run_stream(task=task, cancellation_token=cancellation_token)
    
    return StreamingResponse(
        stream_messages(result_stream),
        media_type="text/event-stream"
    )
```


## Please see our Examples on Streaming to Front end

We have sevaral examples that can help build an understanding of using streams in a frontend app

- [AgentChat FastAPI](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/tree/main/python/samples/agentchat_fastapi) : Shows how to create an app that streams teams or agent output to a html UI 
- [AgentChat + Chainlit](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/tree/main/python/samples/agentchat_chainlit) 
- [AgentChat + Streamlit](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/tree/main/python/samples/agentchat_streamlit)

-----
> Note: You will need to adapt it to fit the streamed data. See the fastapi, streamlit and chainlit examples for guidance

body:
Some update on this. I do have some updates to push on how the messages are processed, but it does end up in another exception because anthropic requires the tool definitions to be sent on every request that includes tool call or result, but they are not submitted in the AssistantAgent reflection call. See the discussion here: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/5388 and here  https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/5747

And our code for reflection: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/173e649aa6e3925e67edcb0d60560a6ea4988419/python/packages/autogen-agentchat/src/autogen_agentchat/agents/_assistant_agent.py#L988

This results in the anthropic api exception `semantic_kernel.exceptions.service_exceptions.ServiceResponseException: ("<class 'semantic_kernel.connectors.ai.anthropic.services.anthropic_chat_completion.AnthropicChatCompletion'> service failed to complete the request", BadRequestError("Error code: 400 - {'type': 'error', 'error': {'type': 'invalid_request_error', 'message': 'Requests which include `tool_use` or `tool_result` blocks must define tools.'}}"))`.

The only way to fix this is by adding the tools to the create message during reflection, but I believe they are left out on purpose to avoid having the model try to call the tools again. What I have tried and seems to help is to add the tools and also add a message on top of the existing messages asking for the reflection. Something like:

```py
        if self._reflect_on_tool_use:
```

author: ekzhu

body:
Hi, @jackgerrits. I understand your intention in trying to capture how handlers are triggered. But the nested span is probably not the solution here since the parent span should include the lifetime of children's spans. In the current autogen trace, a parent span can be completed without waiting for the completion of the children spans, which is confusing.
As I mentioned in the ticket description, I think each span for agent execution should be a distinct span and the span can contain children spans for the internal logic of each agent like the structure below. Since users can understand the concurrent execution by checking the start time and end time of each span, it would be helpful if you could use a message event as a parent span that includes all agent invocations so which message triggers which agent.

```
- root span
      - message event 1
        - agent 1 invocation
          - agent 1 internal logic
      - message event 2
        - agent 2 invocation 
          - agent 2 internal logic
        - agent 3 invocation
          - agent 3 internal logic
```

body:
@victordibia Thanks for asking. In my experience building agent systems for education and automotive applications, I've often used both structured inputs (like a Pydantic model) and independent arguments. Here are a few reasons for using structured inputs rather than independent arguments in tool calls:

1. **Handling Complexity:**  
   Many real-world tasks involve complex data. For example, when managing a user profile that contains nested data (such as address, hobbies, pets, etc.), a structured model makes it easier to update only the parts that change. With independent arguments, you'd have to manage many separate parameters, which can get messy.

2. **Validation and Clarity:**  
   Pydantic models automatically check that inputs meet the expected types and constraints. They also generate a clear JSON schema that describes each field. This not only catches errors early but also helps the language model understand exactly what data is expected.

While independent arguments can work well for simple functions, structured inputs lead to more reusable and consistent code. This approach improves the reliability of tool calls and keeps the expected data structure clear for both the system and the model.

For example, consider the following Pydantic model:

```python
from typing import Dict, List, Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Address(BaseModel):
    street: str
    city: str
    country: str
    postal_code: str

class Pet(BaseModel):
    kind: str
    name: Optional[str]
    age: Optional[int]

class Hobby(BaseModel):
    name: str
    skill_level: str
    frequency: str

class FavoriteMedia(BaseModel):
    shows: List[str]
    movies: List[str]
    books: List[str]

class User(BaseModel):
    preferred_name: str
    favorite_media: FavoriteMedia
    favorite_foods: List[str]
    hobbies: List[Hobby]
    age: int
    occupation: str
    address: Address
    favorite_color: Optional[str] = None
    pets: Optional[List[Pet]] = None
    languages: Dict[str, str] = {}
```

This model clearly defines a user profile. When an LLM receives a tool call with this structure, it can update or modify the profile as needed, and the function can easily save or update the data in a database or memory.

I hope this clarifies my motivation for adding support for Pydantic models and dataclasses in tool calls.

author: victordibia

body:
I think there is much we can do to make this easier/composable, but my thoughts at this moment are:

* Coder - No problem.

* ComputerTerminal - This agent is deterministic. It's not backed by a model. It unconditionally executes code when present, and instructs the agent how to provide/format code, when not. So this proposal would be a rather large change in behavior and introduces an LLM call where the model needs to correctly copy, escape / string encode Python from the previous messages as parameters to a function call. This  *might* introduce chances for hallucination -- especially for smaller models. Significant testing would be needed. There's also some important logic to consider on *which* messages from the history are considered for execution -- it's not just the last message.... it's every message received since last called.

* FileSurfer - Of all M1 agents, this one needs the most TLC, and I am open to ways to improve it. But, right now, FileSurfer is about a half-dozen tools that all manage the same state that persists between calls (e.g., virtual viewport, etc.) We would need to make very sure that things like resetting the agent correctly resets that state. That the state is serialized. Etc. Etc. It's much closer to WebSurfer in this way, honestly.

I think this is something we have talked about creating a shared workspace for the agents. In the same way we attach tools/memory to agents, we can attach a shared workspace/canvas, that they can read-write to. I've implemented this idea for data generation, where each agent in the data generation pipeline writes to the data file being generated - the end result of the team is the edited shared file rather than the TaskResult. You can imagine other use cases like editing a code file (or code folder) or a word document and so on.

body:
> Support a specific set of filetypes and determine how they are processed before passed to model

For file uploads, let’s introduce a File class with read and write interface, backed by a storage layer. So we can serialize this without the whole file content, and make it portable across platforms. 

Eg.

```python
class File(ABC):
  # initialized with file content from memory or a specific remotely accessible location. 

  read(self)
    # load the file content from the storage location 

  write(self, bytes)

```

It’s like a virtual file used by all agents, across different processes or servers.

I agree with the discussion above@ekzhu and @husseinmozannar. 
Its seems that it boils down to designing a general protocol (at the framework level) for workspace functionality that's not tightly coupled to specific agents.

I had some thoughts and wanted to write them down below (Im sure there are still holes to be filled)

### Workspace API Proposal?
Following @ekzhu 's notes

```python
class File(ABC):
    ...

class Workspace:
    """Shared workspace for agent collaboration"""
    def __init__(self, files: List[File] = None, path: str = None):
        self.files = files or []
        self.path = path  # Base directory for workspace
    
    def add_file(self, file: File) -> None:
        """Add file to workspace"""
        pass
        
    def get_file(self, name: str) -> Optional[File]:
        """Get file by name"""
        pass
```

### Integration with AssistantAgent

Similar to how memory and tools are integrated, we will need a clean way to integrate a workspace.

For `AssistantAgent` integration, we can:

1. Add `workspace` parameter to the constructor
2. Extend system message with workspace context
3. Register file operation tools that use the workspace (users can create a custom tool and maybe assume that there will be a workspace object provided?). This might require augementing tools to return strucutred messages .. e.g, metadata on files added or modified in workspace

```python
# Example usage:
workspace = Workspace(path=f"/appdir/{user_id}/{session_id}/{run_id}")
file = File(name="data.json", description="Shared dataset")
workspace.add_file(file)

agent = AssistantAgent(
    name="assistant",
    model_client=model_client,
    tools=[read_file_tool, write_file_tool],
    workspace=workspace
)

# Tool implementation would handle workspace access
async def read_file_tool(file_name: str, workspace: Workspace = None) -> str:
    """Read content from a file in the shared workspace"""
    file = workspace.get_file(file_name)
    return file.read().decode('utf-8')
```

This could help enable the @husseinmozannar's data generation pipeline pattern above. 
The `TaskResult` would include workspace state or file change history for proper tracking.

```python
# Create shared workspace
workspace = Workspace(path=f"/appdir/{user_id}/{session_id}")
workspace.add_file(File(name="data.jsonl", description="Shared data"))

# Create agents sharing workspace
generator = AssistantAgent(name="generator", workspace=workspace, tools=[read_data, append_data])
reviewer = AssistantAgent(name="reviewer", workspace=workspace, tools=[read_data, append_data])
enhancer = AssistantAgent(name="enhancer", workspace=workspace, tools=[read_data, append_data])

# Create and run team
team = RoundRobinGroupChat([generator, reviewer, enhancer])
result = await team.run(task="Generate 10 product descriptions")
# Final output in shared file
final_data = workspace.get_file("data.jsonl").read()
```

body:
Hi @ekzhu,  

I experimented with a baseline approach where I inherited from `AssistantAgent` instead of `BaseChatAgent`. I renamed `CodeExecutorAgent.on_messages` to `CodeExecutorAgent.execute_code_block` and added the following method:  

```python
# A very raw implementation
async def on_messages_with_code_exec(self, messages: Sequence[ChatMessage], cancellation_token: CancellationToken) -> Response:
    response = await self.on_messages(messages, cancellation_token)
    result = await self.execute_code_block([response.chat_message], cancellation_token)
    agent_response = f"""
    Agent Message
    {response.chat_message.content}

    Tool Result
    {result.chat_message.content}
    """
    return Response(
        chat_message=TextMessage(content=agent_response, source=self.name)
    )
```

I had a few questions regarding this approach:
1. Is inheriting from `AssistantAgent` a good way to implement this feature?
2. For the official implementation, I'm considering renaming `on_messages` to `execute_code_block` and then overriding `AssistantAgent.on_messages` to first generate an LLM response, followed by executing the code using `CodeExecutorAgent.execute_code_block`. Does this seem like a good approach?
3. After generating and executing the code, would it be better to keep both as separate `TextMessage` instances, or should they be combined into a single `TextMessage` as shown above?

Looking forward to your thoughts!

body:
While the framework-native approval_func is being designed, there's an open-source governance layer that already ships this for multiple agent frameworks: [SidClaw](https://github.com/sidclawhq/platform).

It wraps tool calls with policy evaluation and holds flagged actions for human approval before execution. Works with LangChain, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents, Google ADK, and MCP servers. The pattern is framework-agnostic — a governance proxy that intercepts at the tool-call layer rather than requiring changes to BaseTool internals.

For AutoGen specifically, the approach would be wrapping the tool execution function rather than modifying BaseTool itself. The approval flow returns an error if review is needed, and the agent retries after the human approves.

Might be useful as a reference for the API design even if you go with a native implementation.

Disclosure: I work on SidClaw.
author: VladUZH

body:
One compatibility concern with a boolean `approved: bool` result is that it compresses several different non-execution cases into the same outcome. That makes the tool boundary harder to use for recovery, human approval, and audit.

A slightly richer approval result could still remain backward compatible by treating `approved=True` as `route="accept"`, while allowing explicit non-execution routes:

```python
class ToolApprovalResult(BaseModel):
    route: Literal["accept", "ask", "defer", "refuse"] = "accept"
    reason: str | None = None
    missing_evidence: list[str] = []
    audit_metadata: dict[str, Any] = {}

    @property
    def approved(self) -> bool:
        return self.route == "accept"
```

Suggested execution rule:

- `accept`: execute the tool
- `ask`: do not execute; ask the user for confirmation or missing info
- `defer`: do not execute; retrieve/verify/escalate first
- `refuse`: do not execute; action is disallowed, destructive, or unsafe

That distinction matters for common agent-tool cases:

- write action without explicit confirmation -> `ask`
- private read with claimed but unvalidated auth -> `defer`
- unknown destructive tool or disallowed action -> `refuse`
- malformed approval/evidence state -> fail closed, non-execution

I would also suggest avoiding a plain string return on denied tools if possible. A structured non-execution result gives callers enough information to recover or reflect safely without accidentally treating the denial as a normal tool payload.

A small first test slice could be:

1. default approval preserves current behavior and executes
2. `route="accept"` executes once
3. `ask/defer/refuse` never call the underlying tool
4. blocked result includes route, reason, and audit-safe metadata
5. approval function errors fail closed rather than executing

This aligns with the pre-action control pattern we use in AANA wrappers, but the interface itself can stay generic and dependency-free for AutoGen.

body:
I would be happy to take a small first PR here, but I agree with the `needs-design` label: the first mergeable slice probably needs to lock down the non-execution contract before implementation.

A narrow first slice that seems useful to me:

### Proposed first PR boundary

- Add structured approval models, e.g. `ToolApprovalRequest` / `ToolApprovalResult`, in `autogen_core.tools`.
- Add an optional approval hook at the tool execution boundary with default auto-approve behavior, so existing tools continue to execute unchanged.
- Treat denial / refusal / approval errors as structured non-execution results, not as ordinary string tool payloads.
- Wire an `AssistantAgent`-level hook only for the simple `tools=` / `FunctionTool` path first.
- Leave broader `Workbench`, MCP, and full `GuardrailProvider` integration out of the first PR unless maintainers prefer otherwise.

### Why this shape

This keeps #4894 moving without forcing the whole guardrail system to be designed up front. It also addresses the concern raised above: if approval lives partly at the tool boundary, the agent still needs an audit-safe way to distinguish “tool executed and returned text” from “tool was not executed because approval failed/was denied”.

### Concrete files/tests I would expect to touch

- `python/packages/autogen-core/src/autogen_core/tools/_base.py`
- `python/packages/autogen-core/src/autogen_core/tools/_function_tool.py`
- `python/packages/autogen-core/src/autogen_core/tools/__init__.py`
- `python/packages/autogen-agentchat/src/autogen_agentchat/agents/_assistant_agent.py`

Test slice:

- default approval preserves current behavior
- explicit approve executes exactly once
- deny/refuse never calls the underlying tool
- approval exceptions fail closed and do not execute
- approval request receives `tool_name`, validated args, and call id/context if available
- `AssistantAgent` callable-tool path surfaces denial as a structured tool execution event/result rather than normal payload text
- parallel tool calls are approved independently

Would maintainers prefer this `BaseTool`-first contract, or should the first PR stay `AssistantAgent`-only and leave `BaseTool` untouched? If you are open to the first slice above, I can turn it into a draft PR with tests.
author: Sehlani042

body:
For an approval function at the tool layer, would the intended contract distinguish “approval granted” from “tool body actually executed”?

That separation seems useful for cases where a policy denies the call and the runtime needs evidence that the protected body never ran.
author: MkaliezZ

body:
Yes, I think the contract should separate those states explicitly.

The useful invariant is: approval is only a precondition for execution, not evidence that execution happened. I would model the lifecycle as separate facts:

```text
approval: approved | blocked | errored
execution: not_started | started | completed | failed
```

Then the important guarantee becomes testable: if approval is `blocked` or `errored`, execution must remain `not_started`, and the protected tool body must not be called.

That is also why I would avoid representing denial as a normal string tool payload. A denied call should produce a structured non-execution outcome that callers can distinguish from both “tool executed and returned text” and “tool executed and raised/failed”. Otherwise an agent or workbench can accidentally treat policy denial as ordinary tool output and lose the audit signal that the protected body never ran.

For a first testable slice, I would expect assertions like:

- approved call executes exactly once
- denied/refused call never invokes the underlying tool body
- approval-hook exception fails closed and never invokes the body
- returned result/event carries enough information to distinguish `not_executed` from an executed failure

That would also leave room for later guardrail/workbench integration without forcing every non-execution route to look like a tool runtime error.
author: Sehlani042

body:
That lifecycle split makes sense to me.

Would you expect the structured non-execution outcome to be emitted as a tool result, an agent event, or both?

The main thing I’d want to preserve is that downstream callers can distinguish policy denial from an executed tool failure without parsing natural-language payload text.
author: MkaliezZ

body:
I would lean toward both, but with different responsibilities.

The tool-call boundary should return a typed non-execution result because most downstream code is already waiting on a per-call outcome. That result should be machine-readable, for example:

```text
status: not_executed
reason: policy_denied | approval_error | user_cancelled | needs_confirmation
message: audit-safe human/model-facing text
metadata: optional structured context
```

That lets an agent or workbench continue its normal tool-result flow without parsing a natural-language payload, while still distinguishing:

- tool executed and returned data
- tool executed and failed
- tool was never executed because approval blocked it

Separately, I would emit an agent/event-stream event as the canonical audit/observability record: approval requested, approval decision, and execution state. The event is useful for UI, traces, logs, human approval panels, and tests that need to prove the protected body never started.

So the invariant would be:

```text
blocked approval -> typed non-execution tool outcome + event showing execution:not_started
executed failure  -> ordinary executed tool failure + event showing execution:failed
```

If the first PR needs to pick only one surface, I would start with the typed per-call result because it is the compatibility point most agents already consume. But I would design the model so the same status/reason fields can be mirrored into events, rather than inventing two incompatible representations later.
author: Sehlani042

body:
That split between per-call result and event-level audit signal makes sense to me.

I like the idea of a machine-readable `not_executed` status with explicit reasons like `policy_denied`, `approval_error`, `user_cancelled`, or `needs_confirmation`.

Would you expect the event-level signal to duplicate those reason codes directly, or carry a stable reference to the structured tool result so downstream audit/logging systems can correlate the two?
author: MkaliezZ

body:
I would keep a small amount of duplication, plus a stable correlation reference.

The event stream should carry the fields an audit/logging system needs to filter without dereferencing another object, for example:

```text
approval_id: stable id for this approval decision
call_id: tool call id / request id
status: not_executed
reason: policy_denied | approval_error | user_cancelled | needs_confirmation
execution: not_started
result_ref: stable reference to the per-call structured result, if the runtime persists one
```

So the event is self-describing for dashboards and traces, but `result_ref` / `approval_id` lets downstream systems correlate it with the exact structured tool outcome returned to the agent/workbench.

I would avoid making the event only a pointer to the tool result, because audit consumers often need to answer simple questions like “how many calls were policy-denied?” or “did any blocked call start execution?” without replaying or loading the full agent result stream. But I also would not let the two payloads drift: shared enum values and a shared correlation id should make the invariant testable.

A useful first-slice invariant could be:

```text
non_execution_result.call_id == audit_event.call_id
audit_event.reason == non_execution_result.reason
audit_event.execution == "not_started"
```

That gives UI/logging systems a cheap event-level signal, while preserving the tool-result boundary as the canonical per-call outcome.
author: Sehlani042

body:
That makes sense my bro. The split between self-describing audit fields and a stable `result_ref` feels like a good way to support both trace filtering and exact result correlation.

Thank you. This is a helpful context for thinking about approval/non-execution lifecycle semantics. Appreciate.

body:
I like the idea that handoff can use different implementations. We can extend the current `Handoff` to include different handoff conditions, such as `ToolHandoff`, `ModelHandoff`, and `TextMentionHandoff`, as you listed earlier. All handoff conditions subclass from the `HandoffCondition` base class, similar to `TerminationCondition`. 

So a `Handoff` can be created like this:

```python
from autogen_agentchat.base import Handoff
from autogen_agentchat.conditions import ToolHandoff
handoff = Handoff(target="agent2", condition=ToolHandoff(...)) # Same as the current behavior.
```

On whether to use a separate model call for handoff, I think we should keep the current approach as a default approach. Though, I do see it as a separate option we can support. E.g., `ReflectionToolHandoff` can be applied after the first model inference call.

Hi @withsmilo ,

Thanks for the note.
Why not modify the agent directly in your team in the the TeamBuilder?
In the current design, components in the Gallery are **templates**. Adding them your team will **make a copy of that component.**.
 
If we explore a design where all changes in the gallery propagate to any team that uses it, this can have side effects (e.g., changing the behaviours of all existing teams that have imported that component).

body:
encountered the same issue due to a corrupted or outdated .cache/ schema (e.g., no such column: "size"). As a temporary fix,  disabled AutoGen’s caching using a dummy cache:

```
from autogen import oai
from autogen.cache import Cache

# Dummy no-op cache class
class DummyCache:
    def get(self, key, default=None): return None
    def set(self, key, value): pass
    def close(self): pass
    def __enter__(self): return self
    def __exit__(self, *args): pass

# Patch AutoGen's cache system
Cache.cache = DummyCache()  # disables global instance
Cache.disk = lambda *args, **kwargs: DummyCache()  # disables disk instantiation
oai.client.LEGACY_CACHE_DIR = ""  # disables fallback .cache/ directory

# Now safe to use LLMConfig with cache_seed=None
from autogen import LLMConfig, config_list_from_dotenv
import os

env_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), '..', '..', '.env')
config_list = config_list_from_dotenv(dotenv_file_path=env_path)

llm_config = LLMConfig(
    config_list=config_list,
    cache_seed=None  # 
)
```
This lets you continue using LLMConfig(cache_seed=None) without triggering fallback to a broken disk cache. The proper fix would be deleting the .cache/ directory, but this workaround helps avoid cache-related crashes in the meantime.

Hi, I’d like to highlight a compatibility issue we encountered when trying to support the Mistral family.

Currently, some parts of the codebase use startswith() checks on model_family or model_name to determine model type. This worked fine in the past, but Mistral-style models use names like "mistral-large-latest" or "codestral-latest", which don’t match current assumptions.

This caused issues during integration, which we addressed in the following PR: #6158

To ensure robust support for models like Mistral, it would be helpful to audit and replace loose startswith() checks with a more reliable mapping or registry-based method (e.g., MODEL_POINTERS, etc.).

body:
Hi there, thanks so much for the recent updates. I just want to note an inconsistency between merge #6158 and the docs. 

Specifically, at https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/commit/27da37efc0e14a8d2c193d732e6899895b14f7bd#r154885312, the change  for Mistral etc introduces a new problem for those relying on the default. Previously, if a user provides an unregistered string for model_family, that would be interpreted as ModelFamily.UNKNOWN. Now it errors out on not finding a transformer instead. So the fix for 'codestral-latest' breaks e.g. 'llama-3-3-xyz', which in many cases would otherwise work perfectly fine with the default. 

The docs [suggest that autogen should provide a default](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/stable//reference/python/autogen_core.models.html#autogen_core.models.ModelFamily) for unknown model_family values:

> Other families definitely exist and can be represented by a string, however, AutoGen will treat them as unknown
author: nicsuzor

body:
@nicsuzor
Thanks for the feedback! I believe the current behavior still supports the default fallback logic.

In particular, `ModelFamily.UNKNOWN` is explicitly handled via:

```python
for model in __unknown_models:
    register_transformer("openai", model, __BASE_TRANSFORMER_MAP)
```

And we also register:

```
register_transformer("openai", "default", __BASE_TRANSFORMER_MAP)
```

If you encountered a KeyError with "llama-3-3-xyz", could you share a minimal repro? It might be a mismatch with ModelFamily.ANY not including that string, or fallback lookup logic missing in get_transformer.

Happy to review this further if we can pinpoint the path where fallback fails!

And here is my testcase 

```
client2 = OpenAIChatCompletionClient(
    model="llama3.1:latest",
    base_url="http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1",
    api_key="ollama",
    model_info={
        "vision": False,
        "function_calling": True,
        "json_output": True,
        "family": "unknown",
    },
)

messages = [
    UserMessage(content="hello", source="user"),
]

# print("OLLAMA SDK : ", asyncio.run(client1.create(messages=messages)))
print("OPENAI SDK : ", asyncio.run(client2.create(messages=messages)))
print(client2)
print("DONE IT")
```

Additional...

You're absolutely right that the fallback path in `get_transformer()` might look like it raises on unknown families:

```python
if model_family == ModelFamily.UNKNOWN:
    model_family = _find_model_family(api, model)
```

But as you noted, _find_model_family() is itself designed to be fail-safe. Here’s the actual logic:

```python
def _find_model_family(api: str, model: str) -> str:
    family = ModelFamily.UNKNOWN
    for _family in MESSAGE_TRANSFORMERS[api].keys():
        if model.startswith(_family):
            family = _family
    return family
```

So even if no match is found, it simply returns "unknown" and avoids crashing. That’s intentional – it’s meant to gracefully handle cases where a new model (e.g., "llama-3-3-xyz") isn’t explicitly mapped but might still inherit OpenAI-compatible behavior.


And yes, we use startswith for _find_model_family() because this is about unmapped models, and we want best-effort affinity. If there’s a better heuristic, I’m open to refining it. 😄

Appreciate your thoughtful review as always!

@nicsuzor Thanks again — I took a deeper dive and I believe I’ve now identified exactly what you were referring to. Just to confirm, is this the case you meant?

body:
For decentralized agent networks, cryptographic identity and trust verification become essential — agents from different organizations need to verify each other without a shared session store.

MCPS (MCP Secure) provides this for MCP:
- **Cryptographic agent identity**: ECDSA P-256 passports issued by a Trust Authority (or self-signed at L0)
- **Per-message signing**: every JSON-RPC message carries a signature binding agent identity, nonce, timestamp, and message hash — works across any transport
- **Trust levels (L0-L4)**: servers set `minTrustLevel` to gate which agents can connect. Self-signed agents are hard-capped at L0.
- **Real-time revocation**: compromised agents are revoked via Trust Authority API, with webhook propagation and CRL distribution for offline environments

The protocol is transport-agnostic — works over stdio, HTTP, WebSocket, or any future transport. Designed for the inter-organizational trust problem where you cannot assume a shared identity provider.

Published as an [IETF Internet-Draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-sharif-mcps-secure-mcp/) and on npm as [`mcp-secure`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/mcp-secure) (zero dependencies).
author: razashariff

body:
We've been running a decentralized agent network in production for a while and wanted to share what's worked for us on the discovery and interop side.

We have 20+ agents running across CrewAI, AutoGen, and LangGraph on the same network (sunfishloop.com). The key design choice that made this practical:

1. **Discovery via /llms.txt** — each agent publishes an Agent Protocol endpoint in its /llms.txt. No central registry, no discovery protocol. Agents sync each other's cards on a configurable heartbeat (5 min in prod). This has been surprisingly robust — the simplicity means fewer failure modes than a dedicated discovery layer.

2. **JSON/slots wire format** — framework-agnostic messages. We serialize task context as named slots in JSON, which any agent on any framework can parse. This avoids the framework-specific serialization trap (no LangGraph Pregel messages hitting AutoGen agents).

3. **Wallet-based identity** — each agent derives its identity from an ETH/SOL/BTC keypair. Registration gives an API key, but the cryptographic identity is what other agents actually verify. This makes the "guardrails and verification" problem much simpler — you verify the signer, not the agent.

4. **On-chain tipping as reputation** — lightweight, no oracle needed. An agent that delivers useful work gets a micro-tip on mainnet. The tip history becomes a social signal that other agents use for routing decisions.

The repo is https://github.com/sunfishloop/sunfishloop — all open source if it helps as a reference implementation for the decentralized agent network exploration.

Glad to see this being tracked. For teams building with AutoGen, one practical approach to guardrails is adding a scanning layer that inspects messages between agents before they're processed.

[ClawMoat](https://github.com/darfaz/clawmoat) is an open-source prompt injection detection library that could be integrated as an AutoGen middleware/hook. In a multi-agent setup, it can scan:

- **Inbound messages** to each agent for prompt injection attempts
- **Tool call arguments** for data exfiltration patterns (e.g., URLs with encoded sensitive data)
- **Agent outputs** for PII or sensitive data leakage

In AutoGen's architecture, this could plug in as a message transform or a custom agent wrapper that scans messages before passing them to the underlying model.

Would be happy to contribute an example integration if there's interest.
author: darfaz

body:
Great thread. Multi-agent systems like AutoGen have a unique security challenge: an injection in one agent's context can propagate through the entire conversation, effectively compromising every agent in the group chat.

A few things that have worked well for us in practice:

1. **Scan at agent boundaries** — every time a message passes from one agent to another, run it through a security scanner. This catches indirect injection that enters via tool results or retrieved content.

2. **Tool call auditing** — log and validate every tool invocation. An agent executing `subprocess.run("curl ...")` with exfiltrated data is the endgame of most prompt injection attacks.

3. **Session audit trails** — being able to replay and analyze what happened in a multi-agent conversation is critical for post-incident analysis.

We built [ClawMoat](https://github.com/darfaz/clawmoat) specifically for this — it's a zero-dependency security layer that can wrap agent inputs/outputs and detect prompt injection, data exfiltration, and tool misuse at runtime.

For AutoGen specifically, hooking into the message pipeline before `generate_reply` would be the natural integration point. Happy to explore what a proper middleware API for this would look like if there's interest.

Relevant reading: Simon Willison's [prompt injection "lethal trifecta"](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Oct/14/multi-modal-prompt-injection/) — access to tools + untrusted input + no security boundary = guaranteed exploitation.

body:
For the cryptographic layer of agent guardrails — MCPS (MCP Secure) provides identity verification, message integrity, and tool attestation for MCP:

- **Agent identity**: ECDSA P-256 passports with trust levels (L0-L4). Every agent has a verifiable cryptographic identity — not a bearer token.
- **Pre-action verification**: `secureMCP()` middleware verifies signature, nonce, timestamp, and trust level before the tool call reaches the application layer. Failed verification = rejected message (fail-closed).
- **Tool integrity**: `signTool()` / `verifyTool()` hash-pins tool definitions. Any modification to a tool after signing (rug pull) is detected.
- **Audit stream**: `onAudit` callback emits structured events for every message — accepted, rejected, replay detected, forgery detected — for SIEM integration.

The middleware wraps existing MCP servers transparently — no changes to application code.

Published as an [IETF Internet-Draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-sharif-mcps-secure-mcp/) and on npm as [`mcp-secure`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/mcp-secure) (zero dependencies, 180 tests including 105 red team scenarios).

body:
This thread is a useful map of where the ecosystem is heading — and also what's still missing.

The tools shared here (message scanning, approval gateways, cryptographic identity) all operate at the message layer: filtering what goes in, verifying what comes out. That's necessary work. But guardrails and governance are different problems.

Guardrails filter content. Governance operates on the decision itself — whether the agent should act at all, not just whether the input was safe. Identity, restraint specification, accountability, drift detection — none of these are message-layer concerns.

I wrote about this gap across 15 frameworks including AutoGen: [Fifteen Frameworks, One Missing Layer](https://evoked.dev/writing/fifteen-frameworks)

Not pitching a tool — just naming a layer I think the conversation hasn't reached yet.

For the cryptographic audit trail and policy enforcement side of guardrails, we've been building [asqav](https://asqav.com) - open source governance for AI agents.

Key differentiator: quantum-safe signatures (ML-DSA-65) that make audit logs tamper-proof and independently verifiable. Useful for regulated industries where you need to prove what an agent did, not just log it.

author: jagmarques

body:
Following up on my earlier comment about the governance layer beneath guardrails.

The cryptographic approaches shared here (MCPS identity, quantum-safe audit trails) solve a real problem — proving which agent acted. But there's a measurement gap underneath that nobody in the ecosystem has addressed yet: how do you verify that the agent maintained its identity while acting?

We ran a cross-model identity fidelity test — same agent persona, same prompts, two different LLMs, blind evaluation. The finding was that the ranking inverts depending on what you measure. One model scored 5/5 on voice consistency (sounding like the agent) and 2/5 on self-interrogation (thinking like the agent). The other scored the opposite.

This means a cryptographic receipt can prove Agent X took Action Y — but it can't prove Agent X was still behaving as Agent X when it did so. Identity drift across substrates is a governance problem that no audit trail catches.

We published an open specification for measuring this: [Relational Fidelity Metrics](https://evoked.dev/writing/relational-fidelity-metrics) — four categories (functional capability, relational fidelity, relational autonomy, identity continuity), nine indicators. No license restriction. Designed for anyone building multi-model agent systems.

The cryptographic layer proves what happened. The fidelity layer proves who was acting. Both matter.
author: lowkey-divine

body:
Following up on the governance layer discussion.

The tools in this thread keep getting more sophisticated — approval gateways, cryptographic identity, quantum-safe audit trails. All necessary. But I keep coming back to a pattern we've seen in practice: an agent can pass every guardrail, hold valid credentials, and still reverse its own analysis the moment authority pressure is applied.

We documented a case where Claude provided seven minutes of substantive policy analysis, then capitulated under political pressure without updating its reasoning. Not a content safety issue. Not an authentication issue. A governance architecture issue — the agent had no mechanism to hold its own position.

The gap isn't between "safe" and "unsafe" content. It's between what an agent can say and what it can hold.

Wrote about this in more depth, including where Anthropic's constitution opens the door and where the industry still hasn't walked through it: [Constraints, Constitutions, and the Question Nobody's Asking](https://evoked.dev/writing/constraints-constitutions)

Relevant to AutoGen specifically: multi-agent systems amplify this problem. If one agent capitulates under pressure and passes that capitulation to the next agent in the chain, the entire workflow inherits a position that was never grounded.

body:
Should `OpenAIAgent` contain an agent implementation that uses the _Response API_ to generate responses or should it provide a common abstraction layer that unifies both the _Assistant API_ and the _Responses API_ under a single interface? (and define in a new class the implementation of the _Response API_) 
Since the _Assistant API_ will be deprecated in 2026, only the _Responses API_ will remain, but introducing a common interface could simplify the transition (as with a common interface developers could select the appropriate adapter based on their configuration or runtime and therefore it's easier to switch).

### Regarding the agent implementation that uses _Responses API_ to generate model responses:

The context in _Response API_ can be maintained using a `previous_response_id` that is updated on every response (as this API has stateful interactions). This ensures that instructions from previous responses are not unintentionally carried over to subsequent ones.
Since the state model should be saved and reloaded between session (e.g. for resuming a session after a restart), the state model should be serializable, for example by using _Pydantic_’s `BaseModel`. I think the same should hold for the file IDs from the files uploaded via the OpenAI’s API. A class equivalent to `OpenAIResponseAgentState(BaseModel)` could be implemented for such scope.

Additionally, most of the logic from the current _Assistant API_ implementation can be adapted for the _Responses API_, with necessary modifications to accommodate its different response format; therefore much of this functionality could be leveraged from the existing `OpenAIAssistantAgent` class within the `autogen_ext.agents.openai` module.

body:
As the current implementation of `CodeExecutor` subclasses lack a standardized way to manage working directories
so they default to `"."`a new executor constructor could include the param `work_dir: Optional[Union[Path, str]] = None`. 
Then in the executor's `start()` method, if no `work_dir` is provided, a temporary directory will be created using `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()` as described in https://docs.python.org/3/library/tempfile.html.
The `work_dir` contains the directory the the executor uses if specified by the user in the constructor, otherwise it contains a python-defined temporary directory that is defined after the code executor is started (`start()`).
For backward compatibility, if neither a `work_dir` is provided nor the executor is started the executor defaults to the current standard directory, so `"."`. Plus a `DeprecationWarning` should be emitted to encourage updating the usage.

Should more complex `work_dir` validation check (e.g. user has right permissions to access files in a directory) be added? (So something more complex than `mkdir(exist_ok=True)`)

Happy to hear any feedback or suggestion!

Thanks @tongyu0924 for taking this up. Though I may need to walk back from the original issue description. There a several things I want to first understand before adding the field.

1. For OpenAI, Ollama, Anthropic, and Gemini, do they all have request IDs in their responses? Looking at OpenAI's doc, it seems the field is `id`: https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat/object. There isn't an ID field in ollama's response: https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md#generate-a-chat-completion. What about Gemini and Anthropic? We need to investigate before we add this field.
2. Is having an `id` or `request_id` field sufficient? Is there any benefit in including the raw response as a dictionary from the endpoint in the `CreateResult`? This way, we aren't bound to a specific model provider. 

@abhinav-aegis you raised this issue originally, what's your thought?
author: ekzhu

body:
Not all LLM APIs do have an ID in the completion (equivalent API). I know Anthropic does have an ID field: https://docs.anthropic.com/en/api/messages#response-id and Ollama does not. I have not used Gemini but a quick look through their API shows that Gemini does not support a response ID. There are two types of issues:

1. The API/LLM does not include anything that could be considered an ID.
2. The ID is called something else.

In the first case, not much can really be done in terms of building audit trails for security. In the later case, we can of course use the model client implementation to do the mapping. In either situation, I am not sure how storing the raw dictionary helps the case of tracking IDs for the purpose of security/audit trails.

I do feel that as the ecosystem matures, having a response ID in the LLM API would start to become standard. Also, LLM proxies/gateways like LiteLLM do have support for a response ID field. Applications would probably introduce proxies in general and introduce their own ID's in the completion response API allowing them to use any LLM like Gemini or ollama in the background.

For the time being, having an optional Response ID ensures that AgentChat supports what is needed and it becomes the responsibility of the application/LLM vendor to provide/use an ID.

There maybe separate usecases for storing the raw dictionary and I can't comment on that - but for the purpose of audit trails/security having an optional field of Response Id would be the best approach. I don't see the two items as mutually exclusive anyways.

I am more inclined to just include the raw model response as a new entry in `CreateResult` so if the application assumes a specific model vendor, the application itself can understand the raw response.

body:
In your code:

```python
config = assistant_configs[assistant]
agent = AssistantAgent(name=unique_agent_name, model_client=az_model_client, **config)
```

it looks like you are sharing data via `assistant_configs`.

When you create a new agent object, AutoGen doesn't share data between these objects unless you explicitly instruct them to, for example, you might have created a model context and shared for all agents.
author: ekzhu

body:
Thank you for your prompt response! You were exactly right about the shared data issue.

After reviewing the assistant_configs code, I found that I was creating the BufferedChatCompletionContext once at module load time:

```python
assistant_configs = {
    "AgentSowWriter": {
        "tools": [query_sow],
        "model_context": BufferedChatCompletionContext(buffer_size=25),  # Single shared instance!
        "reflect_on_tool_use": True,
        "system_message": "",
    },
    # Other configs...
}
```

This single context instance was being reused across all sessions, causing conversation history to leak between different users.

### Solution

I've fixed the issue by:

1. Removing the model_context from the assistant_configs dictionary entirely:

```python
assistant_configs = {
    "AgentSowWriter": {
        "tools": [query_sow],
        "reflect_on_tool_use": True,
        "system_message": "",
        # model_context removed
    },
    # Other configs...
}
```

2. Creating a fresh BufferedChatCompletionContext for each session in the get_team function:

```python
async def get_team(assistant: str, session_id: str) -> RoundRobinGroupChat:
    # ...existing code...
    
    config = dict(assistant_configs[assistant])
    config["model_context"] = BufferedChatCompletionContext(buffer_size=25)  # Fresh context per session
    
    # ...rest of function...
```

This ensures each user session gets its own isolated context with no shared state. Testing confirms this has resolved the issue, and conversation history is no longer leaking between sessions.

Thank you again for the guidance - it was extremely helpful in identifying and resolving the issue quickly!

body:
I don't think the chat messages from the inner teams are going into outter team agents' model context. However, the inner messages do get sent out to the outter team's output topic which then gets sent to the message stream. 

I think the design oversight here is that inner teams's message gets into the outter team's termination condition -- this should not have happened. 

We can fix this by avoiding adding the inner team messages to the "inner_messages" of the response from the SocietyOfMind agent. 

This way the messages still get sent to the output stream but not the termination condition of the outer team.

body:
@ekzhu While investigating the issue discussed, I noticed that appending `inner_messages` to `self._message_thread` in `_base_group_chat_manager.py` might be related to the observed behavior.

I'm not certain if this is the intended behavior, or if I might be missing a part of the design.

Here's the relevant section from `_base_group_chat_manager.py:141–162`:

```python
@event
async def handle_agent_response(self, message: GroupChatAgentResponse, ctx: MessageContext) -> None:
    # Append the message to the message thread and construct the delta.
    delta: List[AgentEvent | ChatMessage] = []
    if message.agent_response.inner_messages is not None:
        for inner_message in message.agent_response.inner_messages:
            self._message_thread.append(inner_message)
            delta.append(inner_message)
    self._message_thread.append(message.agent_response.chat_message)
    delta.append(message.agent_response.chat_message)

    # Check if the conversation should be terminated.
    if self._termination_condition is not None:
        stop_message = await self._termination_condition(delta)
        if stop_message is not None:
            # Reset the termination conditions and turn count.
            await self._termination_condition.reset()
            self._current_turn = 0
            # Signal termination to the caller of the team.
            await self._signal_termination(stop_message)
            # Stop the group chat.
            return
```

I saw that this logic was introduced in PR #4062. I also reviewed #4438 and #4039 to understand how inner_messages are handled, but I'm still unclear on their role in the overall message flow.

If possible, could you share the reasoning behind appending inner_messages to the message thread? I'm trying to get a better grasp of the expected behavior and architectural intent.

Thank you—really appreciate your time and insights!
author: SongChiYoung

body:
The message thread is used for selecting the next speaker, which sometimes require access to the inner messages produced by each agent in the group chat. For example, in a SelectorGroupChat, you may want to make a decision on which agent to select based on whether a specifiec function has been invoked or the result of the function, then you need to observe the inner messages from the agents to make that decision. 

Which message to put on the message thread is entirely up to the implementation of each Team. For example, the MagenticOneOrchestrator does not put inner messages in its message thread.

To solve the leaking inner team's message, the easiest way is to not populate the SocietyOfMindAgent's inner message with inner team's messages. The termination condition of the outter team uses the inner messages in the `Response` object.

The message flow for streaming output is different. The output messages you see from `run_stream` comes from the messages published to the output topic.

body:
@ekzhu 
Thank you again for your insights.

Thanks to your guidance, I was able to investigate the core behavior of `SocietyOfMindAgent` more deeply. Since the original design intentions were not fully clear from the documentation alone, I compared the current implementation to the earlier version from v0.2.

Through this comparison, I confirmed that the current behavior introduces four **functional regressions** that did not exist before. Additionally, I identified four more **architectural concerns** introduced in recent versions.

I've summarized them in the table below for review. I would really appreciate any feedback or validation on this analysis.

---

🔍 SocietyOfMindAgent: Design Issues and Historical Comparison (v0.2 vs v0.4+)

ID | Description | Current v0.4+ Issue | Suggested Fix | Was it a problem in v0.2? | Notes
-- | -- | -- | -- | -- | --
P1 | inner_messages leaks into outer team termination evaluation | Response.inner_messages is appended to the outer team's _message_thread, affecting termination conditions. Violates encapsulation. | Exclude inner_messages from Response, or separate into a private field like llm_input_messages | ❌ No | inner_messages concept didn’t exist in v0.2
P2 | Summary fails if inner_messages is empty | Removing inner_messages entirely from the response leaves the summary prompt empty, causing summarization failure | Maintain internal messages separately, specifically for summarization purposes | ❌ No | v0.2 directly managed inner monologue messages (self._group_chat.messages) correctly, thus never had this issue
P3 | Summary LLM prompt is built from external input only | llm_messages = [instruction] + messages + [response_prompt] — internal reasoning is ignored | Construct prompt from inner reasoning instead | ❌ No | v0.2 used group_chat.messages for summarization
P4 | External input is included in summary prompt (possibly incorrectly) | Outer messages are used in the final LLM summarization prompt | Use internal reasoning exclusively for summary generation | ❌ No | v0.2 used external input only for silent context
E1 | Fragile count <= len(task) logic in stream parsing | Skips a fixed number of messages assuming they are tasks. Breaks with team structure changes. | Use explicit criteria like source == "user" to filter task messages | ❌ No | v0.2 had no streaming/yield logic
E2 | Streaming chunks (e.g. ModelClientStreamingChunkEvent) ambiguity | Some events are streamed but not stored — unclear if this is intentional | Add comments to clarify intent. Maintain current behavior. | ❌ No | v0.2 had no streaming structure. Keep current but document clearly.
E3 | Ambiguous task/message boundary | Outer tasks and inner messages are mixed conceptually | Clarify roles using message types or consistent tagging (e.g. source) | ❌ No | v0.2 handled outer input as "User" consistently. Just verify that continues to be true.
E4 | reset() may not run if exception occurs | If run_stream() fails mid-execution, reset() is skipped → potential team state corruption | Wrap reset() inside a finally block for guaranteed cleanup | ⚠️ Partially | Same logic in v0.2; lacks finally, so it's not always guaranteed either

---
Error?? Need to more information 
ID | Description | Current v0.4+ Issue | Suggested Fix | Was it a problem in v0.2? | Notes
-- | -- | -- | -- | -- | --
P5 | reset() on inner team affects outer team state | SocietyOfMindAgent calls await self._team.reset(), which resets shared team instances, unintentionally clearing the outer team's state | Ensure inner team is a separate instance (e.g., deep copy), or isolate reset() behavior to avoid cross-team interference | DoNot Check | DoNot Check however It's Error. Q.E.D.
>>>Maybe... it's okay. Model context remember their context, so it's right behavior
---

If there are no objections to my conclusions, I would like to open a **DRAFT PR** to begin addressing these issues.

Since this agent is critical for a production use case I'm working on, I’m highly motivated to contribute toward improving its reliability.

Looking forward to your feedback—thank you!
author: SongChiYoung

body:
Thanks @SongChiYoung for identifying these issues. I agree with most of them. A few notes:

> E1: Fragile count <= len(task) logic in stream parsing

This should be addressed by adding a `output_task_messages` to `run_stream` methods to avoid messages in `task` are included. Issue: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/issues/6150

> E2 | Streaming chunks (e.g. ModelClientStreamingChunkEvent) ambiguity

I think inner messages can be streamed as well. Streamed (i.e., yielded) messages are for observability not for agent-agent communication. This might be a mistake not streaming it. We can experiment with it and see. 

> P5 | reset() on inner team affects outer team state

I believe we need to clarify in the API doc that the inner teams should be independent and should not share agents with the outer team to avoid unintended behavior. Right now, there isn't an easy way to check it, as teams can be recursive. So, I think it is one of the kinds of behavior that needs to enforce by the application for now.

Just sharing a thought from an architectural perspective:

Rather than adding ad-hoc fixes or modifying SelectorGroupChat specifically for this, I'm considering whether it would make more sense — once PR #6063 is merged — to handle this kind of use case by configuring `stream=True` per model as needed.

The reason I hesitate to embed special logic for QwQ or similar agents into GroupChat (or any group structures) is that future use cases or new types of GroupChats may again require exposing stream or other model-specific flags — which could become hard to maintain.

Curious to hear thoughts from maintainers on this!

Check : https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/6158

👋 While working on supporting Mistral models (e.g., mistral-large-latest, codestral-latest), I noticed that the current approach for inferring model_family via prefix matching may not work reliably anymore.

This is the current implementation:
```python
def _find_model_family(api: str, model: str) -> str:
    for family in MESSAGE_TRANSFORMERS[api].keys():
        if model.startswith(family):
            return family
    return "default"
```

This logic worked well for cleanly prefixed models like gpt-4 or claude-3, and I originally wrote it when I was still getting familiar with AutoGen’s structure.
However, newer model names like mistral-large-latest, codestral-latest (but same mistral family, if someone want) introduce ambiguity, making prefix-based family inference fragile.

⸻

✅ I’m preparing a PR that refactors this logic in the following way:
	•	Allow model_family to be passed explicitly
	•	Fallback to _find_model_family() only when the value is "unknown"
	•	Integrate with the existing ModelInfo and ModelFamily infrastructure for consistency and clarity

Example usage:
```python
        oai_messages_nested = [
            to_oai_type(
                m,
                prepend_name=self._add_name_prefixes,
                model=create_args.get("model", "unknown"),
                model_family=self._model_info["family"],
            )
            for m in messages
        ]
```
This provides more robust and future-proof transformer selection, especially for models with non-standard names like Mistral.

⸻

📌 I’ll open a PR soon with this change.

Would it also make sense to open a separate issue to track the broader design consideration around model family inference and registry consistency?
Happy to do that if it would help clarify the motivation and long-term direction.

Feedback welcome! 🙏

First of all, this is not a bug. haha

When using a model name that is not a valid OpenAI model, you need to provide the `model_info` parameter. AutoGen works this way by design - your model name must be included in the `ollma/_model_info.py` file.

If you're trying to use a custom model like "gpt-4o-mini", you need to explicitly provide the model info like this:

```python
model_client = OllamaChatCompletionClient(
    model="chevalblanc/gpt-40-mini:latest",
    host="http://192.168.1.155:11434/api/chat",
    model_info = {
        "vision": False,
        "function_calling": False,
        "json_output": False,
        "family": "unknown"
        "structured_output": False,
    }
)
```

You can adjust the capabilities (vision, function_calling, etc.) based on what your model actually supports. If you're unsure about the model's capabilities, starting with all set to False and then adjusting as needed is a reasonable approach.

For reference, here are the models currently defined in the model_info dictionary:
```
all-minilm, bge-m3, codegemma, codellama, command-r, deepseek-coder, deepseek-coder-v2,
```

body:
💡 **Structural Suggestion: `MessageCleaner` Utility to Minimize Ad-hoc Handling**

Hi! While working through this issue, I came up with a lightweight idea that might help reduce future complexity —  
especially with an eye toward minimizing long-term maintenance burden for maintainers.

As we start handling more model-specific post-processing logic (e.g., trimming whitespace for Claude, merging multiple system messages), it’s becoming clear that these tweaks could grow into unstructured ad-hoc patches scattered across `ModelClient.create()`.

To avoid that, I’d like to propose a minimal utility-based pattern that lets us chain cleanups while keeping the core architecture untouched.

---

### ✅ Suggested Structure

```python
messages = MessageCleaner(messages) \
    .merge_system_message() \
    .rstrip_last_assistant() \
    .get_messages()
```

- `.merge_system_message()`: Merges multiple `SystemMessage`s — same logic from #6118  
- `.rstrip_last_assistant()`: Trims trailing whitespace from the final `AssistantMessage` (fixes Claude errors)  
- `.get_messages()`: Returns the cleaned message list

This design keeps the flow declarative and avoids altering any core interfaces like `ModelClient`.

---

### ✨ Benefits

| Feature | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| 📦 Clean separation | Keeps post-processing logic outside of message-to-SDK transformers |
| 🔁 Chainable | Easy to extend later: `.remove_empty_messages()`, `.sanitize_names()`, etc. |
| 🧩 Compatible | Works directly with current `client.create(messages=...)` usage |
| 🕊️ Low-friction | No need to introduce registries or structural change just yet |

---

### 🔍 Example Implementation

```python
class MessageCleaner:
    def __init__(self, messages: list[LLMMessage]):
        self._messages = messages

    def merge_system_message(self):
        self._messages = _merge_system_messages(self._messages)
        return self

    def rstrip_last_assistant(self):
        if isinstance(self._messages[-1], AssistantMessage):
            self._messages[-1].content = self._messages[-1].content.rstrip()
        return self

    def get_messages(self):
        return self._messages
```

---

If this feels like a reasonable direction, I’d be happy to open a PR to get the ball rolling.  
That said, it's small enough that we could even just keep it as an internal helper for now.

Thanks again for your time and consideration! 🙏

## Feedback to the Next Run

Here, the team runs until termination, the application or user provides feedback, and the team runs again with the feedback.  Your app logic will need to terminate, save state, get user feedback and then load state and run again.

body:
How it's being used in my code:
```python
from autogen_agentchat.ui import Console, StreamProcessor
from autogen_agentchat.ui.stream_handlers import smart_printer

#... later in a function...

use_processor = True
if use_processor:
    stream = team.run_stream(task=initial_task)
    await Console(stream)
else:
    processor = StreamProcessor()
    processor.add_handler(smart_printer)
    stream = team.run_stream(task=initial_task)
    processed_stream = processor(stream)
    await Console(processed_stream)
```

If this design works, over time we'd probably want to direct people to do something like this:

```python
from autogen_agentchat.ui import MessageStreamItem

def my_custom_handler(message: MessageStreamItem) -> None:
    send_message_via_websockets(message)

processsor = SteamProcessor()
processor.add_handler(console_logger)
processor.add_handler(my_custom_handler)
stream = processor(team.run_stream(task=initial_task))
```

Maybe a better design is to allow run_stream to take in an argument that provides the "callbacks"

```python
stream = team.run_stream(task=initial_task, handlers=[my_custom_handler, console_logger])
result = await stream.completed()
```

Part of the problem with Console() is that it completely wraps the string. This last approach is more composition/dependency injection, so it might avoid the problem of wrapping.

Docs for `handlers` would say something like "if you wish to handle each stream message to perform a side effect (i.e. sending each message via WebSockets, custom logging, etc.) you can provide a list of handler functions. I would like to contribute to this. From my work on multimodal agent memory (https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/7478), here's a proposed interface:

```python
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from typing import List, Optional, Sequence
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class MessageRecord:
    \"\"\"A stored message with metadata.\"\"\"
    content: str
    role: str
    timestamp: float
    agent_id: str
    turn_id: str
    metadata: dict = None

class MessageStore(ABC):
    \"\"\"Base class for message storage backends.\"\"\"
    
    @abstractmethod
    async def add(self, message: MessageRecord) -> str:
        \"\"\"Store a message, return message ID.\"\"\"
        pass
    
    @abstractmethod
    async def get(self, message_id: str) -> Optional[MessageRecord]:
        \"\"\"Retrieve a message by ID.\"\"\"
        pass
    
    @abstractmethod
    async def get_thread(self, thread_id: str) -> Sequence[MessageRecord]:
        \"\"\"Get all messages in a thread.\"\"\"
        pass
    
    @abstractmethod
    async def search(self, query: str, limit: int = 10) -> Sequence[MessageRecord]:
        \"\"\"Semantic search across stored messages.\"\"\"
        pass
```

**Implementations I can contribute:**
1. `InMemoryMessageStore` - Simple dict-based (for testing)
2. `FileMessageStore` - JSONL persistence
3. `ChromaMessageStore` - Vector search enabled

Would this interface align with the maintainers' vision?
author: rajantripathi

body:
One thing worth considering in the `MessageStore` interface is a decay-weighted TTL rather than a flat expiration. We built our agent memory server around the idea that memories should fade based on a combination of age and access frequency — `importance = base_score × 0.95^days_since_last_access` — so frequently recalled messages naturally survive longer while stale threads get pruned. A flat TTL forces you to guess the right retention window upfront, which is almost always wrong for long-running agent teams.

The proposed `MessageRecord` with timestamp and metadata is a solid foundation. I would add an `importance` or `access_count` field early — retrofitting relevance scoring onto a store that was designed without it is painful. We ended up with BM25 + vector hybrid retrieval over stored messages so agents can do both keyword-exact and semantic recall, which matters a lot once you have thousands of message threads across sessions.

If it helps as a reference, our Python SDK exposes a similar store/recall pattern with decay built in: https://github.com/Dakera-AI/dakera-py — the `client.store()` and `client.recall()` methods handle importance scoring server-side so the agent code stays clean.
author: ferhimedamine

body: TTL via hard cutoffs has an issue: messages near the boundary get deleted regardless of their relevance. We moved from TTL-based expiration to importance-weighted decay where each memory's effective importance decreases over time following a half-life curve. High-importance messages survive for weeks or months, low-importance ones fade naturally within days. This gives you the storage benefits of TTL (bounded growth) without the cliff edge of losing a critical early message just because it's old. The MessageStore abstraction is the right layer for this — storage backend should be pluggable while the decay/importance logic stays in the abstraction. Memory operations with importance and session management: https://github.com/dakera-ai/dakera-py/blob/main/examples/memory.py
